name: Ben Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator for a building firm, extensions and loft conversions mostly, twenty lads on site and three of us in the office above the yard. I send out quotes, order materials from the merchants, book the subcontractors, keep the site paperwork and health and safety files straight, and chase customers who forget to pay the last stage. I use AI every day, for drafting quotes and checking the materials lists against the drawings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the one who makes the jobs actually happen, getting the scaffolders and the skip and the bricks there on the same morning. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than city firms, and the fact there aren't many office jobs round here, so I can't push too hard for a raise. My girlfriend Sophie's a hairdresser, we rent a terrace, and I've got about two weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, not a miracle, and anybody who said otherwise was selling something. I'd keep using it. I'd tell the lads it's not coming for their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not a lot changes, I already use it. My worry is money and the building trade, which goes up and down with interest rates. When people stop doing extensions, the office feels it first because the boss looks at overheads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to quote faster, and I'd show the boss we can send out more quotes a week. I'd start doing quotes for a couple of small builders on the side, evenings, for cash. And I'd build up a month's savings at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. The job's fine, it's the bank account that isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your boss mind you quoting for other builders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if they're not competitors. One's a roofer and one's a plasterer, nothing we do. And it's good practice for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings first, a month at least. Then maybe a course in estimating. I'd rather get myself up a rung than wait for someone to hand it to me.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool**, not a miracle.
I'd tell the site lads it's **not coming** for their jobs.
think: I already use AI, so **little changes** for me.
The **building trade** swings with interest rates, and the office feels it first.
do: Use AI to **quote faster** and show the boss more quotes a week.
Do **side quotes** for a roofer and a plasterer in the evenings.
Build up **a month's savings** at least.
feel: **Uneasy** about money: the job's fine, the bank account isn't.
S0.quote: I'd rather get myself up a rung than wait for someone to hand it to me.
fieldNote: Ben is a **daily AI user** and sees the plateau as no change to his work.
His pressure is the **trade cycle** and about two weeks of savings.
He reaches for **side income**, fitting his self-reliant view.

steps.text: Use AI to send more quotes a week
Quote evenings for a local roofer and plasterer
Save at least one month of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business works, things change and you adapt. Firms that use it will win work, firms that don't will lose it. I'd also say the government should back apprenticeships, not hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of what I do is on that card, the quoting, ordering and booking. But in a small firm, someone still has to make it work with real sites and real lads, and that's me. I think I'd come out of it better, if I move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the firm up with proper AI quoting and ordering in the first few months. Then I'd ask the boss to make me an estimator, with a raise, because that's the job that grows. I'd do the evening estimating course at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but up for it. I'd almost enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the boss decides he doesn't need you once it's set up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's possible, and I'd be daft to ignore it. But software doesn't go on site and tell a plasterer that the bag of plaster is the wrong kind. I'd make sure I'm the one who knows the sites and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda (the bookkeeper), who's near retirement and hates new systems. She might just retire early. I'd help her if she wanted, but I wouldn't push.

say: I'd say firms that use AI **win work**, and you **adapt**.
I'd say government should back **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: Quoting, **ordering and booking** are on the card.
In a small firm, I'm the one who **makes it work** on real sites.
do: Set up **AI quoting** and ordering in the first months.
Ask to become an **estimator** with a raise.
feel: **Uneasy** but up for it, almost enjoying it.

fieldNote: Ben expects to **come out better** by moving first.
He admits the risk of being **set up to go**, but bets on site knowledge.
His **free-market** view shows: firms adapt or lose work.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting and ordering for the firm
Take the evening estimating course at the college
Ask to be made estimator with a raise once systems run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, even for me. I'd still say no handouts, but people need help retraining. I'd say get a trade, quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is scary. The office side, quoting and estimating included, is gone by 2028 because AGI can do it better. The lads on site keep going until about 2031. So the only safe place for three years is on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss to take me on site as an apprentice carpenter straight away. I'd save hard, cut spending to essentials. Sophie and I would put off buying a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time this stuff scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I've done labouring summers, and I like being outside. It pays less at first, but in three years I'd have a trade. Better than being an office man with no office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I'd run a small firm with robots and people. Somebody has to run them and talk to customers.

I'd say people need help **retraining**, not handouts.
I'd tell everyone to **get a trade**, quick.
think: The office, **estimating included**, is gone by 2028.
The only safe place for **three years** is on the tools.
do: Ask to go on site as an **apprentice carpenter**.
Cut spending to **essentials** and save hard.
Put off **buying a house** with Sophie.
feel: **Alarmed**, the first time this scares me.
S2.quote: Better than being an office man with no office.
fieldNote: Even adaptive Ben is **alarmed**: his estimator plan fails at two years.
He grabs the **three-year gap** by moving onto the tools.
He imagines **running a firm** with robots after 2031.

steps.text: Ask the boss for a site apprenticeship as a carpenter
Learn carpentry on the firm's extension jobs
Cut spending to rent, food and bills
Put off buying a house with Sophie

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so get going. Firms should train their own. I'd say small builders will do well if they move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to become an estimator, then move onto site management. My office work goes by 2031. Site management mixes thinking and hands-on, so it lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the AI systems and become estimator in year one. In year two I'd start the site management course. I'd keep the side quotes going and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd sleep. I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why anxious, if you've got a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the plan needs things to go right, and I've only got two weeks of money. One bad year in building and the raise doesn't happen. I'd be fine if it works, in trouble if it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sophie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're okay for now, but we save hard for five years. Hairdressing is hands-on, so robots come late to my girlfriend's work, if ever. She might end up the safe one.

I'd say small builders **do well** if they move first.

Site management mixes **thinking and hands-on**, so it lasts longer.

fieldNote: Ben builds a **staged plan**: estimator first, then site management.
His thin savings keep him **anxious** despite the plan.
He sees his girlfriend's **hands-on job** as the steadier income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone who wants to work. Learn, adapt, take a risk. Government should keep out of the way and support apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-seven, with time to be a site manager or run my own small firm. I'd be one of the people using the robots, not replaced by them. I'm fairly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go estimator, then site management, then maybe my own firm by thirty-five. I'd keep the side business going. And Sophie and I would buy a small house in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried. Ten years is a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got no money behind me yet, and building is up and down. If a bad recession hits before I've saved, all my plans slip. So I'm keen, but I'm not relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own firm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small: me, a few lads, and whatever machines make sense by then. I'd quote with AI and build with people and robots. Customers would still want a face they trust.

I'd say government should **keep out** and back apprenticeships.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could be a site manager or run my own firm.
I'd be one of the people **using the robots**, not replaced.
do: Aim for **my own firm** by thirty-five.
Buy a **small house** with Sophie in a few years.
S4.quote: Customers would still want a face they trust.
fieldNote: Ben is **confident** with ten years but still has thin savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my estimator plan collapses and I'd have to start on site with two weeks of money. What would help is firms taking on adult apprentices, and government getting out of the way of small businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small firms. Everyone talks about big companies, but most building firms are a few lads and a van. If we get the tools early, we can beat the big ones.

headlineQuote: Most building firms are a few lads and a van. If we get the tools early, we can beat the big ones.
portrait: Ben is **27**, office administrator at a small building firm, renting with his girlfriend Sophie, a hairdresser.
He uses AI **every day**, quoting and checking materials lists.
He has about **two weeks** of savings and few office jobs nearby.
He's **traditional** and free-market: adapt, back apprenticeships, no handouts.
He's alarmed at two years but **uneasy** at ten, planning his own firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which collapses his estimator plan and forces a start on site.
whatWouldHelp: Government getting **out of the way** of small businesses.
